title: Scaling Topologies: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling in Cloud & AI Workloads
description: Master scalability patterns for modern .NET & AI systems: stateless API scale-out, stateful session routing, distributed caching with Redis, read replicas with EF Core, and autoscaling topologies on Kubernetes / Azure.

data.text: The Architecture of Scalability in Modern Systems

Scalability is the ability of a system to maintain acceptable latency and throughput as workload increases by dynamically adding compute or memory resources. In enterprise .NET and AI systems, scaling demands a nuanced hybrid approach: vertical scaling (scaling up) provides instant relief for write-heavy relational databases and large in-memory caches, while horizontal scaling (scaling out) provides fault-tolerant, elastic, and economically viable growth for web APIs, document ingestion pipelines, and agent orchestration engines.

data.text: Stateless API Design & Shared Data Protection

To scale an ASP.NET Core application horizontally behind a load balancer, instances must share zero local state. Any in-memory session, local file uploads, or local ASP.NET Core Data Protection keys (used to encrypt auth cookies and anti-forgery tokens) will cause random authentication failures when requests alternate between nodes.

data.title: Configuring Distributed Data Protection & Redis in ASP.NET Core
data.content: This configuration stores cryptographic keys in Azure Blob Storage with Key Vault encryption and uses Redis for shared distributed caching.

data.text: Database Scale-Out with EF Core Read Replicas

Relational databases cannot scale writes horizontally across multiple nodes without distributed locking overhead. The industry standard is vertical scaling of the primary node for ACID writes, coupled with horizontal read replicas for queries.

cards.title: Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)
cards.description: Increase CPU cores, RAM, and NVMe disk speed on a single machine.
pros: No distributed concurrency or network latency issues
Simple operations with a single deployment target
cons: Harsh hardware ceilings and exponential cost curves at high tiers
Single point of failure during hardware reboots or maintenance
Cannot scale beyond the largest available machine size

cards.title: Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out)
cards.description: Add multiple identical application instances behind a load balancer.
pros: Virtually unlimited elastic scaling capacity in public clouds
High availability: failing nodes are automatically recycled
Linear cost scaling — add capacity incrementally
cons: Requires strictly stateless application tier architecture
Demands distributed caching, locks, and external session state
More complex operational tooling (Kubernetes, KEDA, YARP)

data.text: Traditional CPU-based autoscaling fails for AI workloads. An ingestion worker processing large PDFs might be network-bound or waiting on OpenAI rate limits while CPU remains at 15%. Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA) scales pods based on message queue depth (RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, or Redis list size).

data.caption: Autoscaling Metrics and Scaling Dimensions
rows: Concurrent HTTP Requests / Active SSE Streams (>50 per pod)
Pending queue messages in Azure Service Bus (>5 jobs per pod)
Scale pods from 0 to 10 instances (Scale to Zero)
Vertical resize cache tier or add Redis cluster shards
Spin up additional read replicas and enlarge write compute

data.title: Horizontal Scaling Readiness Checklist
items: No in-memory state or static dictionaries used for user sessions or cached data
ASP.NET Core Data Protection configured with external blob storage and Key Vault
Database connection pools managed using PgBouncer or Azure Database Connection Pooler
Read queries routed to database read replicas with NoTracking enabled
Health checks implement proper Readiness vs Liveness probe semantics
KEDA or equivalent event-driven autoscaling configured for background job workers

data.title: Summary & Next Steps
points: Stateless application architecture is the non-negotiable prerequisite for horizontal scaling.
Shared distributed state (Redis, Blob Storage) decouples compute from persistence.
Event-driven autoscaling (KEDA) handles bursty AI ingestion better than traditional CPU metrics.
Next, we learn how to benchmark and profile .NET code using BenchmarkDotNet and diagnostic tools.
data.takeaway: Design every service to be stateless from the start: compute should be ephemeral, disposable, and horizontally elastically scalable.
